sentences: He was too happy, however, to need much attention; and, luckily for the others, the business of love-making relieved them from a great deal of his company.

senses.learner: because of good luck.
examples: But, luckily, he came back again in ten minutes' time, and then we all set out.
she is luckily too poor to be an object of prey to anybody.

sentences: You have no compassion on my poor nerves."

senses.gloss: any bundle of nerve fibers running to various organs and tissues of the body
senses.learner: a bundle of very thin threads (fibres) that runs to the organs and other parts of the body.
examples: The doctor said the fall had damaged a nerve in his arm.

senses.gloss: the courage to carry on
senses.learner: the courage to keep going.
examples: Halfway up the cliff she lost her nerve and could not go on.

senses.gloss: impudent aggressiveness
senses.learner: rude, pushy boldness that shows no respect for others.
examples: He broke my window and then had the nerve to ask me for money.

sentences: He begged pardon for having displeased her.

senses.gloss: accept an excuse for
senses.learner: to accept someone's excuse for something they did.
examples: never had she before been so much disposed to pardon his interference in the views of his friend.

senses.gloss: grant a pardon to
senses.learner: to officially free someone from the punishment for a crime.
examples: The governor pardoned the prisoner, and he walked free the next day.

sentences: The path just admitted three.

senses.gloss: a way especially designed for a particular use
senses.learner: a way made especially for one particular use.
examples: The path just admitted three.
before she could strike into another path, she was overtaken by Wickham.

senses.gloss: a course of conduct
senses.learner: a way of behaving that someone follows.
examples: He chose the path of honesty, even when it cost him his job.

senses.gloss: a line or route along which something travels or moves
senses.learner: the line or route along which something travels or moves.
examples: The storm destroyed every house in its path.

senses.gloss: an established line of travel or access
senses.learner: a fixed, usual way of travelling to or getting into a place.
examples: The guide showed us the usual path from the village to the lake.

sentences: I am not qualified to form one.
Nay, were your friend Lady Catherine to know me, I am persuaded she would find me in every respect ill qualified for the situation."
"Perhaps," said Darcy, "I should have judged better had I sought an introduction, but I am ill-qualified to recommend myself to strangers."
Shall we ask him why a man of sense and education, and who has lived in the world, is ill-qualified to recommend himself to strangers?"

senses.gloss: meeting the proper standards and requirements and training for an office or position or task
senses.learner: having the training and meeting the standards and requirements needed for a job, position or task.
examples: I am not qualified to form one.
she would find me in every respect ill qualified for the situation.

senses.gloss: limited or restricted; not absolute
senses.learner: limited in some way; not complete or total.
examples: The plan won only qualified approval from the committee.

senses.gloss: holding appropriate documentation and officially on record as qualified to perform a specified function or practice a specified skill
senses.learner: having the right official papers and being on record as allowed to do a certain job or use a certain skill.
examples: He is now a qualified pilot, with his licence on record.

senses.gloss: contingent on something else
senses.learner: depending on something else.
examples: Their offer is qualified on your passing the final exam.

senses.gloss: restricted in meaning; (as e.g. ‘man’ in ‘a tall man’)
senses.learner: having its meaning narrowed by another word, as 'man' is in 'a tall man'.
examples: In 'a tall man', 'man' is a qualified noun, because 'tall' narrows its meaning.

sentences: They could describe an entertainment with accuracy, relate an anecdote with humour, and laugh at their acquaintance with spirit.

senses.learner: a short telling of something that happened, especially something in a person's life.
examples: They could describe an entertainment with accuracy, relate an anecdote with humour, and laugh at their acquaintance with spirit.
Lady Catherine was generally speaking--stating the mistakes of the three others, or relating some anecdote of herself.

sentences: Her father had been an attorney in Meryton, and had left her four thousand pounds.

senses.gloss: a professional person authorized to practice law; conducts lawsuits or gives legal advice
senses.learner: a person whose job is the law, who is allowed to work in it and who takes cases to court or gives advice about the law
examples: Her father had been an attorney in Meryton, and had left her four thousand pounds.

sentences: Before Elizabeth had time for anything but a blush of surprise, Mrs. Bennet instantly answered,--

senses.learner: a sudden redness that comes into your face, for example when you feel embarrassed, guilty, ashamed or shy
examples: Once or twice she could discern a faint blush; but in general Charlotte wisely did not hear.
Their eyes instantly met, and the cheeks of each were overspread with the deepest blush.

senses.learner: a pink colour, especially in the cheeks, that is seen as a sign that someone is healthy

senses.learner: a pink or red powder that people put on their cheeks as makeup
examples: She brushed a little blush onto her cheeks before going out.

to say the truth, I was too cross to write.
